item.title: Expression of White and Gray Matter Autism Functional Network Connectivity Signatures in Infancy
item.description: arXiv:2610.40839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Functional connectivity studies have provided valuable insights into altered brain organization in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, most functional connectivity studies focus exclusively on either gray matter (GM) regions or white matter (WM) tracts and examine specific age groups, rather than investigating their functional interactions across brain development. This limits our understanding of how GM-WM functional interactions evolve developmentally and may obscure important aspects of brain network organization in ASD. We combined integrated WM+GM functional network connectivity (FNC) with brain-wide risk scores (BRSs) to quantify ASD-associated pattern expression in ABIDE I/II and an independent infant cohort. We employed a NeuroMark framework with predefined WM and GM intrinsic connectivity networks templates, to estimate subject-level FNC. First, we identified two distinct patterns of altered WM+GM FNC in ASD: GM-related hypoconnectivity centered on the paralimbic network and WM-GM hyperconnectivity centered on the frontal network. These findings highlight the involvement of higher-order cognitive networks and the importance of WM-GM functional interactions in characterizing ASD-related connectivity alterations. Second, infants with a higher familial likelihood of autism exhibited greater mean expression of ASD-associated FNC patterns than those with a lower familial likelihood, as quantified by BRS. These group-level findings do not establish developmental persistence or predict diagnostic outcomes at the individual level.
item.dc:creator: Qiang Li, Jingyu Liu, Zening Fu, Armin Iraji, Sarah Shultz, Vince D. Calhoun

item.title: Hyperbolic embedding of higher-order simplicial networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.41684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many biological interactions involve groups rather than pairs, as when several proteins assemble into a multi-protein complex. Simplicial complexes naturally capture these collective interactions. Existing hyperbolic embeddings represent network hierarchy and similarity through a few interpretable coordinates, but rely only on pairwise links: they cannot distinguish three units engaged in a common interaction from three units connected only in pairs. We introduce here the hyperbolic higher-order (HHO) embedding, which embeds a simplicial complex into the Poincar\'e disk, while incorporating its group interactions. The hyperbolic area of the triangle spanned by three interacting nodes then measures how compactly their interaction is represented. Testson synthetic and real-world networks, including a co-authorship network and the protein interaction network of \textit{Escherichia coli}, show that HHO reduces the hyperbolic area of triangles representing simplices relative to those obtained from pairwise network embeddings. HHO also recovers node groups more accurately than pairwise embeddings and a weighted-clique alternative, with performance competitive with Euclidean embeddings, while providing a low-dimensional representation that can be analyzed with the tools of network geometry.
item.dc:creator: Martin Guillemaud, Vito Latora, Mario Chavez

item.title: Explainable AI-Driven Neural Activity Analysis in Parkinsonian Rats under Electrical Stimulation
item.description: arXiv:2502.12471v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by motor dysfunction and abnormal neural oscillations. This study combined graphene-based cortical stimulation with an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework to investigate spatial and frequency-related features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals were recorded before and after stimulation and classified using EEGNet and DeepConvNet. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) and DeepLIFT were applied to identify frequency bands and recording channels contributing to the classification. The anatomical locations of these channels were mapped onto a cortical map. XAI analyses were performed separately for each animal to examine individual attribution patterns. Our XAI analysis revealed frequency-band- and region-specific contributions to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Our approach provided complementary insights into the features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation ECoG classification alongside PSD-based analyses. These findings highlight the potential of combining graphene-based cortical stimulation with explainable deep learning to identify classification-relevant features across frequency bands and cortical areas in pre- and post-stimulation recordings.
item.dc:creator: Jibum Kim, Hanseul Choi, Gaeun Kim, Sunggu Yang, Eunha Baeg, Donggue Kim, Seongwon Jin, Sangwon Byun

item.title: Lattice-Based Pruning of Recurrent Neural Networks via Poset Modeling: A Corrected Theory and a Matched-Sparsity Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2502.16525v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Magnitude pruning of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) ignores how information flows between neurons. An earlier version proposed to model RNN dependencies as a partially ordered set (poset) and to retain the meet-irreducible elements of its dependency lattice. By Birkhoff's representation theorem, the meet-irreducible ideals of a finite poset are in bijection with its elements, so retaining them retains everything; the critical-set criterion used earlier selects precisely the elements comparable to all others, of which a dense recurrent layer has none. Condensing a thresholded dependency graph into strongly connected components yields a well-defined dependency order, a graded order score and an acyclic pruning rule; for Cohen-Grossberg networks and LSTMs, acyclic pruning makes local stability decompose over modules. For a 128-unit LSTM pruned at matched sparsity on row-wise and chunked sequential MNIST (three seeds, equal training budgets), the original rules remove every recurrent weight or equal random column pruning; the order score is no better than degree, PageRank or norm; trained weights show little directional bias; and imposing acyclicity from initialisation costs 2.1 and 10.5 percentage points at 50% and 90% sparsity. In the networks studied, order structure must be imposed rather than discovered.
item.dc:creator: Rakesh Sengupta

item.title: Building functional and mechanistic models of cortical computation based on canonical cell type connectivity
item.description: arXiv:2504.03031v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neuronal circuits of the cerebral cortex are the structural basis of mammalian cognition. The same qualitative components and connectivity motifs are repeated across functionally specialized cortical areas and mammalian species, suggesting a single underlying algorithmic motif. Here, we propose a perspective on current knowledge of the cortical structure, from which we extract two core principles for computational modeling. The first principle is that cortical cell types fulfill distinct computational roles. The second principle is that cortical connectivity can be efficiently characterized by only a few canonical blueprints of connectivity between cell types. Starting with these two foundational principles, we outline a general framework for building functional and mechanistic models of cortical circuits. Finally, we show that the compressed and generative representations of connectivity entailed by this framework are particularly amenable to automatic search through gradient-free optimization, providing a concrete first step towards modelling the evolution of functional neural circuits.
item.dc:creator: Arno Granier, Katharina A Wilmes, Mihai A Petrovici, Walter Senn

item.title: Message interaction dynamics covary with brain volume across mammalian connectomes
item.description: arXiv:2505.15477v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Brain network communication models typically assume that signals propagate independently, despite the high network density and small diameter of mammalian connectomes, where interactions among simultaneously propagating messages are likely. We investigate these interactions using the copy-spread-annihilate (CSA) model, a synchronous Markovian message-passing process in which messages spread through the binarized network while undergoing collision-dependent deletion. Simulations on a large comparative dataset of mammalian connectomes show that CSA dynamics produce robust positively-skewed lognormal distributions of message survival across species. Despite using only binary network topology without spatial embedding, message survival accounts for over half of the variance in brain volume across mammal species and outperforms a broad range of established graph-theoretic measures and an alternative communication model with interacting messages. These relationships persisted when measured paths could not revisit nodes. Degree-preserving switch randomization weakens the relationship between message survival and brain volume, indicating that higher-order structural organization contributes to the observed scaling law. We describe a mechanistic explanation of model dynamics that suggests message creation differences among networks shapes message survival. Together, these findings suggest that interactions among propagating messages constitute an important and underexplored determinant of communication dynamics in mammalian brain networks.
item.dc:creator: Yan Hao, Hannah Lax, Marc-Thorsten H\"utt, Daniel J. Graham

item.title: Perceived vertical and eye level as one orientation process: a closed-form account of the Li-Matin combination rules for egocentric space
item.description: arXiv:2607.19681v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Li and Matin (2005a, 2005b) reported three regularities of the induced visually-perceived vertical (VPV), the direction judged upright. For small tilts, a peripheral line shifts it nearly linearly with tilt, two lines combine nearly linearly, and mirror-image tilts cancel. Each line votes at twice its angle, weighted by its strength. The votes' vector sum $c_1$ is the first circular moment of the doubled angles; half its angle, $\phi=\tfrac12\arg c_1$, is the induced vertical, a stimulus axis, not the judged upright. This is the orientation order-parameter model (PLUMB). We prove that $c_1$ is, up to a constant factor, the only additive summary of axes (lines without arrowheads) that scales with line strength and turns twice as far as the field rotates. With Li and Matin's own length gain and no per-configuration fit, the model matches their multiline coefficients in-sample. Their data rule out complete summation but not simple averaging for long lines. But a line's effect is fourfold (period $90^\circ$): it reverses past $45^\circ$ (Li and Matin, 2005a; Vingerhoets et al., 2009), and near-horizontal lines shift VPV as near-vertical ones do, which $c_1$ forbids. In a two-harmonic fit to Li and Matin's data, $c_1$ carries an estimated 2--4% of a near-vertical line's slope and a fourfold term the rest. To first order in tilt, for near-vertical segments, the readout equals the committee rule Shavit, Li, and Matin (2026) fit to eight line-array experiments, with its drives read as concentrations. If the half-fields' signals are read as sum and difference, perceived eye level (VPEL) is the difference, recovering Shavit, Li, and Matin's (2013) reversed integration rules; a fourfold term gives the same signals, so this does not single out $c_1$. Re-analysed data (30 observers) show the predicted signs and nulls, an internal check only; the cross-field gain is fitted.
item.dc:creator: A. Y. Shavit

item.title: Critical Flicker Fusion Frequency As An Experience-Restricted Constraint On Visual Temporal Resolution: What Does And Does Not Change It
item.description: arXiv:2607.29068v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Experience-dependent plasticity is fundamental to adaptive behaviour, yet the conditions under which basic sensory timing can be modified in adulthood remain poorly specified. Critical flicker fusion frequency (CFFF), the threshold at which flicker is perceived as continuous, is unusually informative here: what fails to change it is as well documented as what does. We argue that CFFF is best characterised neither as non-plastic nor as held near a physiological ceiling, but as modifiable only by a specific class of experience, not by amount. Repeated testing changes it little, and cognitive training without temporal content and incoherent-motion exposure leave it unchanged regardless of duration. By contrast, perceptual-learning paradigms that repeatedly drive early visual processing of transient signals can raise it. The evidence is graded: strongest for task-irrelevant coherent motion temporally paired with task targets, with one-year retention in a small subsample; weaker for contrast and dot-motion training; and, for flicker training, confined to amblyopic eyes starting below typical values. Three qualifications apply: samples are small; the motion and contrast paradigms were assessed with a small foveal stimulus on a macular pigment densitometer, whose equivalence with standard CFFF measurement is unestablished; and a minority of untrained controls show comparable changes. We examine whether the restriction originates at peripheral, thalamocortical, or cortical levels; available data do not adjudicate between them. Functional arguments for such a restriction are offered as rationales, not evidence. Proposed links to working-memory precision and metacognition are stated as predictions; first tests were largely negative.
item.dc:creator: Natalia D. Rydzenska, Pawel J. Winklewski, Michal W. Blaszczyk-Niezgoda, Anna B. Marcinkowska
